en: Devīgītā: Now begins the first chapter— the seventh book.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"The supreme light manifested upon the crown of the Lord of Mountains."
Tell me that which you previously spoke of at length.

What wise person, drinking the nectar of the discourse on power, would not become dispassionate? For those who drink the [ordinary] nectar of immortality there is death, but for one who hears this, there shall be none.
Vyāsa said:
You are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and you have been instructed by the great-souled ones;
you are fortunate, since you possess sincere devotion toward the Goddess.
Listen, O King, to what occurred in the past: when Satī’s body had been consumed by fire, Śiva wandered in confusion until he came to rest in a certain place.
Free from the appearance of conceptual proliferation, his mind attained to meditative concentration,
that self-possessed one spent his time meditating upon the very form of the Goddess.
The three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, have become bereft of fortune;
the entire universe, with its oceans, continents, and mountains, has been deprived of power.
Joy has withered within the hearts of all;
all the worlds have become indifferent, their minds shattered by anxiety.
They were then constantly submerged in an ocean of suffering, afflicted by diseases,
due to the adverse movements of the planets and the deities.
Because of the true nature of the elemental and divine beings, they became kings.
Now, at that very time, there was a great asura named Tāraka.
The Daitya who has received a boon from Brahmā shall become the leader of the three worlds;
however, he who is the biological son of Śiva shall be your slayer.
Thus, having had his death ordained by the gods of gods, that great asura roared and rejoiced because of the absence of a son born from Śiva’s semen.
Harassed by him and displaced from their own abodes,
all the gods fell into insurmountable anxiety due to the absence of a son born of Śiva’s semen.
Śaṅkara has no wife; how, then, can there be the birth of his son?
For us who are devoid of fortune, how will this task be accomplished?
Thus, all of them, distressed by anxiety, went to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha;
they praised Hari in private, and he spoke a means to them.
Why are you all so anxious, O auspicious ones who are like wish-fulfilling trees?
The Mistress of the World, who dwells on the Jewel Island, is awake.
Our indifference toward that [suffering] arises solely from our own lack of discipline, and not otherwise;
this very instruction was given by the Mother of the World for our training.
Just as a mother feels no compassion for her child whether she is pampering or striking it,
so too does the Mother of the World feel toward the world when she restrains it from virtue and vice.
A son indeed commits offenses at every step;
who else in the world, except for his mother alone, can endure them?
Therefore, go for refuge to that Supreme Mother without delay;
with a sincere state of mind, she will accomplish your purpose.
Having thus instructed all the gods, Mahāviṣṇu,
the lord of the gods, departed quickly accompanied by his own wife and together with the deities.
He went to the great mountain Himavat, the lord of mountains;
and all the gods performed the preliminary rites before him.
O King, those who were experts in the ritual procedures for the *ambā* sacrifice performed the *ambā* sacrifice;
all the gods quickly performed the vows beginning with the third, O monarch.
Some are proficient in meditative concentration, some are devoted to the names [of the Buddhas];
some are intent on the well-spoken verses, and some are eager for the complete recitation of the names.

Some are devoted to the recitation of mantras, some perform ascetic penances such as the *kṛcchra*; some are intent on internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), and some are dedicated to the ritual placement of mantras (*nyāsa*).
With unwearied devotion, they performed the worship of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) by means of the Hṛllekhā mantra;
in this way, O Janamejaya, many years passed by.
Suddenly, on the ninth day of the month of Caitra, on a Friday,
that splendor made known by the Vedas appeared before him.
It was praised from the four directions by the personified four Vedas;
it shone like ten million suns and was as cool as ten million moons.
That supreme light, red in hue and possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
could not be grasped as being above, nor across, nor in the middle.
That, however, is devoid of beginning and end; it is not joined with limbs such as hands, nor is it in the form of a woman, nor in the form of a man, nor both.
O Lord of the Earth, the brilliance [of that light] caused the eyes of those gods to close;
yet, once again taking hold of their fortitude, they looked upon it.
At that moment, he appeared in a divine and captivating female form—
a maiden in the prime of youth with exceedingly beautiful limbs.
Her pair of full, uplifted breasts surpassed the beauty of lotus buds;
her tinkling girdle and anklets resounded with the sound of a network of small bells.
Adorned with golden armlets, bracelets, and necklaces,
and resplendent with a collar set with priceless jewels.
Her hair, dark like a blue bee, shone with the beauty of a slender ketaka flower;
she was lovely with the orb of her hips and adorned by the line of hair upon her body.
Her mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor,
and her lotus-face was adorned with shimmering golden earrings.
Her forehead resembles the orb of the eighth-day moon; her eyebrows are long;
her eyes are like red lotuses; she has a prominent nose and sweet lips.
Her teeth are like jasmine buds, she is adorned with a pearl necklace,
her crown is inlaid with jewels, and she wears the crescent moon as a crest-ornament.
She is resplendent with a mass of hair adorned with garlands of *mallikā* and *mālatī* flowers;
her forehead is marked with saffron dots, and she is graced by three beautiful eyes.
She has four arms holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is three-eyed, wears red garments, and has the luster of a pomegranate flower.
She who is enriched with every elegant ornament and attire, who is saluted by all the gods,
who fulfills all hopes, who is the mother of all, and who fascinates all.
The gods beheld before them their Mother, whose face was bright with grace, whose lotus-face was adorned with a gentle smile, and who was the very embodiment of sincere compassion.
Upon seeing that embodiment of compassion, all the gods prostrated;
their voices choked with tears, they were unable to say anything at all.
Having somehow regained their composure and with their necks bowed in devotion,
their eyes filled with tears of love, they praised the Mother of the World.
The gods said:
"Homage to the Goddess, to the Great Goddess; constant homage to Śivā! Homage to Prakṛti, to Bhadrā; being self-restrained, we bow down before her."

I take refuge in that goddess Durgā, who is fire-colored, blazing with ascetic power, the daughter of Virocana, and who delights in the fruits of karma; homage to you, O Sutarasi, who deliver us across [the ocean of existence]. Dg_1.45 = DbhP_7,31.45.
The gods generated divine speech; animals of every form speak it.
May that cow-like speech, lowing sweetly and yielding for us refreshment and nourishment, come to us well-praised.
We pay homage to Kālarātrī, praised by Brahmā, the power of Viṣṇu, the mother of Skanda,
Sarasvatī, Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa— the purifying and auspicious one.
We know Mahālakṣmī; we meditate upon her as the power of all;
may that Goddess inspire us.
Homage to her whose nature is the Virāṭ, homage to her whose form is the Sūtrātman;
homage to her whose nature is the unmanifest (avyākṛta), homage to the venerable embodiment of Brahman.
We bow to that Sovereign of the World, through whose ignorance the world appears like a snake or a garland in a rope, and through whose knowledge it attains dissolution.
We bow to her whose referent is the meaning indicated by that word, whose nature is the single essence of consciousness,
whose form is indivisible bliss, and who is the ground of the Vedas' ultimate purport.
She is beyond the five sheaths, the witness of the three states,
the meaning indicated by the word "thou" (tvam-pada), and the very nature of the inner self (pratyagātman).
Homage to her whose form is the syllable *praṇava*; homage to her whose embodiment is the syllable *hrīṃ*;
homage again and again to you, compassion itself, whose nature consists of manifold mantras.
Thus praised by the gods, she who dwells on the Jewel Island then spoke with sweet words, like the song of a cuckoo in rut.
The illustrious Goddess said:
"O wise ones, tell me the purpose for which you have gathered here;
I am always the bestower of boons, and I am the wish-fulfilling tree for the desires of my devotees."
While I remain present, what concern can there be for you who are full of devotion?
I shall deliver my devotees from the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.
"O best of the wise, know that this vow of mine is true.
Having heard these words, which were overflowing with love, their minds were filled with satisfaction.
Fearless and free from decay, O King, the gods spoke of their own suffering.
The gods said:
"There is nothing here in the three worlds that is unknown to you."
O Supreme Goddess, who are omniscient and the witness of all,
we are oppressed day and night by Tāraka, the lord of the asuras.
O Maheśvarī, you know that his slaughter was brought about by Brahmā out of inauspiciousness toward Śiva’s body; however, there is no such thing as a wife of Śiva.
What indeed could be said by vulgar people in the presence of the Omniscient One? This has been declared by way of summary; O Ambika, consider the rest for yourself.
"May you possess unwavering devotion at all times toward the lotus-feet [of the Buddha];
this is my primary prayer, while the other is for the sake of [obtaining] a body. (Dg 1.62 = DbhP 7,31.62)
Having heard these words of theirs, the Supreme Goddess spoke:
"That Gaurī who is my own power shall come to be in the Himalayas."
She should be given for the sake of Śiva; she will accomplish your task, provided that you have devotion for her lotus-feet with earnestness.
For the Himalaya serves me with his mind through supreme devotion;
therefore, it is considered pleasing to me that my birth should take place in his home.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words which were exceedingly gracious, Himālaya,
his throat and eyes choked with tears, spoke these words to the Great Queen.
You treat as more important him toward whom you desire to show favor;
otherwise, where am I—a dull, inert pillar—and where are you, whose nature is pure being and consciousness?
O sinless one, it is impossible for you to become my father even through hundreds of births,
nor by means of merits such as the horse sacrifice, nor by merits born of meditative concentration equal to them.
"Today her fame shall spread throughout the world: 'The Mother of the World has become our daughter!
Oh, how blessed and fortunate is this Himālaya! "
But she in whose womb reside millions of world-systems—she alone has become his daughter; who indeed on earth could be equal to her?
I do not know what supreme abode has been prepared for our ancestors, for such as these to dwell in, from whose lineage one like me has arisen.
Tell me how this was given to me out of compassion and full of love,
and likewise describe to me your form, which is established in all the Vedāntas.
O Supreme Goddess, since you yourself are I, please tell me of yoga accompanied by devotion and of the knowledge approved by the Vedas.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of his, Ambā, her lotus-like face serene, began to speak that secret which had been hidden from the Vedas.
Thus ends the first chapter of the Devīgītā;
thus ends the thirty-first chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the second chapter.
The Seventh Section; now the thirty-second chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"May all you immortals listen to the words I am speaking,
by the mere hearing of which one attains my very form."
O Lord of Mountains, formerly I alone existed, and nothing else whatsoever;
that nature of mine is consciousness-awareness, known by the single name of the Supreme Brahman.
Inconceivable, indefinable, incomparable, and free from ailment—
his certain power, established by itself, is renowned as "māyā."
It is not existent, nor is it non-existent, nor does it possess the nature of both due to contradiction;
rather, there is always some entity that exists as a reality distinct from these characteristics.
Like the heat of fire, like the radiance of the sun,
or like the moonlight of the moon— this innate nature of mine is constant.
In that [state], the individual lives of living beings and their karmas circulate;
they become merged without distinction, just as worldly activity ceases in deep sleep.
Through the conjunction with my own power, I have attained the nature of the seed;
yet, due to the obscuration of my own support, that [power] has also come to possess the state of being a defect.
Due to its conjunction with consciousness, it is described as the efficient cause (nimitta);
and due to the transformation of the phenomenal world (prapañca), it is called the inherent cause (samavāyin).
Some call it austerity (*tapas*), some darkness (*tamas*), others the insentient (*jaḍa*);
[others] knowledge (*jñāna*), illusion (*māyā*), the primary matter (*pradhāna*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), or even the unborn power (*śakti*).
Those proficient in the Śaiva scriptures call that "vimarśa" (reflective awareness),
while others who contemplate the true meaning of the Vedas call it "avidyā" (ignorance).
Thus, there may be various names for it in the Vedas and other scriptures;
however, because it is insentient and an object of perception, it becomes non-existent upon the destruction of knowledge.
Consciousness is not an object of perception; if it were an object of perception, it would be insentient.
Furthermore, consciousness is self-luminous and is not illumined by another.
Because of the fault of infinite regress, it is not illuminated even by itself;
there would be a contradiction between the object and the agent. Therefore, it is self-illuminating like a lamp.
O Parvata, know that which is manifest to others to be the illuminator;
for this very reason, the eternity of my nature as perfected consciousness is established.
Because the object of perception varies across the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep,
whereas no variation in consciousness itself has ever been experienced at any time.
If there is an experience of that [object] as well, then that very witness by whom it was experienced remains here as the primordial embodiment of consciousness.
For this very reason, its eternity has been proclaimed by those learned in the true scriptures;
and its nature as bliss is due to its being the object of supreme love.
"May I not cease to be; may I indeed exist"—this [desire] resides in the self out of love.
Since everything else is false, my state of non-attachment is evident. (Dg 2.18 = DbhP 7,32.18)
For this very reason, I maintain that its indefiniteness is likewise established;
moreover, that gnosis is not a property of the self, for if it were a property, the self would be insentient.
The insentience of knowledge has never been observed, nor is it possible;
likewise, it does not possess the property of consciousness, for consciousness is not distinct from consciousness.
Therefore, the Self is always of the nature of knowledge and of the nature of bliss;
it is real, complete, unattached, and free from the web of duality.
Furthermore, through his own māyā conjoined with desire, karma, and so forth,
[he arises] from the latent impressions of previous experiences and from the ripening of time and karma.
And due to a lack of discernment regarding reality, he becomes desirous of creation;
this creation, which is not preceded by conscious intent, has been described to you, O Lord of Mountains.
For this which has been proclaimed by me is my own extraordinary form;
it is unmanifested, unevolved, and is also called "the variegated illusion" (māyā-śabala).
It is proclaimed in all the scriptures as the cause of all causes,
the primordial ground of all principles, and whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
That which is the condensation of all karma, the locus of will, knowledge, and action,
denoted by the mantra syllable *hrīṃ*— that is called the primordial reality (*āditattva*).
From that, space is produced, having the nature of the subtle element of sound;
from that, wind arises, consisting of the essence of touch; and then fire, consisting of the essence of form.
Water consists of the quality of taste; thereafter, earth consists of the quality of smell.
Space has sound as its sole quality, and wind is endowed with both touch and sound.
Fire is said by the wise to have the qualities of sound, touch, and form;
water is traditionally remembered as having four qualities: sound, touch, form, and taste.
Earth possesses five qualities: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell;
from these arose the Great Thread (mahatsūtra), which they call the Liṅga.
That is declared to be the essence of all; this is the subtle body of the self.
It is indeed called the unmanifest causal body, as was stated previously.
In that [subtle body] the form of the seed of the world resides, from which the emergence of the subtle body (liṅga) occurs;
from that, the gross elements arise by way of the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa).
Five [elements] are produced; their specific modes are now described. One should divide each of the previously mentioned elements into two parts.
O Mountain, one should divide each single part of the one into four;
by joining each with its own second part and the other’s second part, they become five each.
And its effect is the body of Virāj, this gross body of the self;
through the sattva-portions residing in the five elements, there arises the emergence of the sense organs, such as hearing and the rest.
O King of Kings, when the sense organs are combined one by one with those [elements],
there arises a single internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which, due to the difference in its functions (vṛtti), is fourfold.
When its function consists of conceptualization and discursive thought, it is designated as "mind" (manas);
and when it perceives with firm certainty, free from the form of doubt, it is known by the name "intellect" (buddhi).
That mind is proclaimed to be of the nature of investigation;
however, through the activity of the self based on the notion of "I," it attains the state of ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra).
From portions of those [elements], the organs of action are known to arise in sequence;
and from each of these, when combined, the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes fivefold.
Prāṇa is in the heart, apāna is in the anus, while samāna resides in the navel;
udāna is in the region of the throat, and vyāna pervades the entire body.
There are exactly five sense organs and five organs of action;
likewise, there is the pentad of vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, together with the intellect and the mind.
This subtle body is what is called my *liṅga*;
the *prakṛti* that is spoken of therein, O King, is traditionally held to be of two kinds.
Illusion (māyā) consists of sentient beings and is ignorance mixed with the [three] qualities (guṇa); that which protects its own locus is called "illusion. (Dg 2.43 = DbhP 7,32.43)
The reflection of that Lord who serves as the original object (*bimba*) within that [mirror] is declared to be the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*), who possesses knowledge based upon his own substrate.
He is the omniscient one, the creator of all, and the performer of grace for all;
yet, O Lord of Mountains, whatever reflection appears within ignorance— // Dg_2.45 = DbhP_7,32.45 //
That very [unmanifested state] is designated as the "living being" (jīva), which is again the locus of all suffering;
here, it is taught that for both [the unmanifested and the living being], there are three bodies through ignorance.
Furthermore, from the identification with the three bodies, there arose again a triad of names:
the *prājña* is the causal self (*kāraṇātman*), while the one possessing the subtle body is the *taijasa*.
The one possessing the gross body is proclaimed as being threefold, known by the name Viśva;
likewise, Īśa is also designated by the terms Īśa, Sūtra, and Virāṭ.
The first is of the nature of individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*), while the supreme is known as the self of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*).
For he is the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*) himself, acting out of a desire to bestow grace upon living beings.
Furthermore, O King, impelled by my power and eternally established within me, he creates the manifold universe, which is the locus of various enjoyments.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Devīgītā—
thus in the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, the thirty-second chapter of the Devīgītā.
Now begins the third chapter.
The Seventh Book: Now the Thirty-third Chapter. The Goddess said:
The entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is fashioned by my power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*);
yet, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even that illusion does not exist as something separate from me.
From the perspective of conventional usage, this very [reality] is renowned as "knowledge" (vidyā) or "illusion" (māyā);
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it does not exist at all—only reality itself exists in its absolute purity.
Having created the entire world, O Mountain, I enter into its midst, accompanied by illusion, karma, and the rest, with the vital breath as my precursor.
If there were no transition to another world, how could it be? For by this very reason, just as various illusory manifestations arise, so do they [the states of existence] come to be.
Just as the space within jars and other such things appear distinct due to the difference in their limiting adjuncts,
so too the sun always illuminates objects such as those that are high or low.
I am not defiled in that same way, nor have I ever been tainted by faults;
it is other people who, through their own intellect, superimpose the agency of cognition and so forth upon me.
The deluded, not the wise, say that the self is karma;
likewise, they speak thus due to the differentiation of ignorance and the differentiation of māyā.
The distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is indeed imagined by māyā alone,
just as the distinction between the space within a jar and the great expanse of space is imagined.

In the same way, the distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is imagined; likewise, the multiplicity of individual selves exists only through māyā and not by its own nature.
Likewise, the multiplicity of Īśvaras is due to *māyā* and not by way of their own nature;
it is differentiated by the diversity of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the aggregates of body, sense-faculties, and so forth.

O Supporter of the Earth, ignorance alone is proclaimed as the cause of the distinction between living beings; no other cause is taught, for it is differentiated by the various latent impressions of the qualities (guṇas).
That illusion is the cause of the differentiation of others, and never anything else;
O Supporter of the Earth, all this is woven across and through me.
I am the Lord, and I am the Sūtrātman; I am also the Virāḍātman.
I am Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; I am Gaurī, Brāhmī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
I am the sun, I am the stars, and likewise I am the Lord of the stars;
I am the very form of beasts and birds, and I am the outcaste and the thief.
"I am a hunter; I am one of cruel deeds; I am a person of virtuous deeds; I am a great man;
even in the forms of woman, man, and neuter, I alone am so—of this there is no doubt."
Whatever object whatsoever is seen or even heard anywhere,
whether internal or external— I pervade all that and remain forever.
There is not a single thing, whether moving or unmoving, that has been abandoned by me;
if there were such a thing, it would be empty, for it would be like the son of a barren woman.
Just as a single rope appears as various things such as a snake or a garland, so indeed do I manifest in the forms of Īśvara and others; there is no doubt in this.
That which is imagined does not appear apart from its substratum;
therefore, this world possesses existence only through my own existence, and not otherwise.
Himālaya said:
"O Goddess of gods, if you have compassion for me, O Goddess, I wish to see this body of the universal aggregate exactly as you describe it."
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of his, all the gods, together with Viṣṇu,
rejoiced with delighted souls, honoring those words.
Then, having understood the intention of the gods, Śivā— the wish-fulfilling cow for her devotees and the fulfiller of the desires of her devotees— revealed her own form.
They beheld the supreme form of the Great Goddess, beyond the transcendent,
of whom heaven is the head and the moon and sun are the eyes.
The directions are said to be his ears, the gods his speech, and Vāyu his breath;
they call the universe his heart, and the earth is remembered as his lower part.
The vault of the sky is the navel-lake, the circle of light is the chest,
Mahārloka is the neck, and Janaloka is known as the mouth.
The world of heat (tapoloka) is the forehead, situated below the world of truth (satyaloka);
Indra and the other [guardians] are the arms, and sound is the ear of the Great Lord.
The two nostrils are the *nāsatya* and *dasra*; smell and the sense of smell are known from memory;
fire is declared to be the mouth; and day and night are the eyelids.
The place of Brahmā is the expansion of the eyebrows; water is proclaimed to be the palate;
taste is declared to be the tongue; and Yama is proclaimed to be the fangs.

The teeth of the Great Lord are proclaimed as the essence of affection (*sneha-kalā*); his smile is *māyā*; his sidelong glance is emission (*sarga*); and the upward-turning of his upper lip is modesty (*vrīḍā*).
Her lower lip is greed; the path of Dharma is her back;
and he who is the creator upon the surface of the earth, Prajāpati, is her generative organ.
The belly of the Great Sovereign Goddess is the oceans, her bones are the mountains;
the channels are declared to be the rivers, and her hair is proclaimed to be the trees.
Childhood, youth, and old age constitute his supreme gait;
the clouds are his hair, and the two twilights are the garments of the All-pervading Lord.
O King, the moon is traditionally held to be the mind of Śrī Jagadambā;
Viṣṇu is her power of cognition (vijñāna-śakti), and Rudra is traditionally held to be her internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
For all the various classes of horses are situated in the hip region of the Lord;
the great worlds, beginning with Atala, have become the lower portion of his waist.
The preeminent gods beheld such a great form,
rich with thousands of garlands of flames and licking with its tongue.
The hero who vomits fire from his eyes with a clattering sound from his fangs,
who wields various weapons, and who is the food for the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
Having a thousand heads and eyes, and likewise a thousand feet;
resembling ten million suns, with a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
All those gods beheld that terrifying and most horrific sight, which caused dread to their hearts and eyes, and they raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
With their hearts trembling, they fell into an insurmountable swoon; even the memory that "this is the Mother of the World" vanished from them. (Dg 3.39 = DbhP 7,33.39)
Then those Vedas that were situated in the four directions of the Great Lord awakened the gods, who had fainted from their swoon, with a most fierce sound.
Then those immortals, having regained their composure and attained that supreme teaching,
stood with eyes filled with tears of love and throats choked with emotion.
With voices choked with tears, they began to offer praise.
The gods said:
"O Mother, forgive our transgression; protect us, the wretched ones born from you."
"O Goddess of gods, withdraw your anger; we are filled with fear at the sight of your form.
What praise could be offered to you here by us, mere mortals and non-gods?"
Even for himself, that which is his own prowess—however great it may be—is indeed unknowable;
how then could it be an object of perception for those born after him?
Salutations to you, O Mistress of the World; salutations to you, whose essence is the Praṇava.
Salutations to you, who are perfected by all the Vedāntas; salutations to you, the embodiment of the syllable Hrīṃ.
Salutation to that Self of All, from whom fire has arisen, from whom the sun and the moon have arisen, and from whom all medicinal herbs have arisen.
And because from him the gods were born, as well as the Sādhyas, birds,
animals, and humans— homage to that one who is the Self of all!
To him from whom come out-breath and in-breath, rice and barley, austerity, faith, and likewise truth,
as well as celibacy and ritual injunction— homage, homage to him!
Salutation to that Self of All, from whom there are seven rays of breath, seven fuel-sticks, seven oblations, and likewise seven worlds.
Since from him the oceans, mountains, and rivers flow forth,
and since all herbs and essences arise from him— to him, salutation after salutation!
Salutation to that Self of All, from whom sacrifice has arisen, as well as initiation, the sacrificial post, the priestly fees, the *ṛc* verses, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman* chants.
Homage to you in front and behind; homage to you on both sides;
homage again and again, O Mother, below, above, and in the four directions.
O Goddess of gods, withdraw this extraordinary form;
show us instead that form which is most beautiful of the beautiful.
Vyāsa said:
Seeing the gods thus terrified, the Mother of the World, that ocean of compassion,
withdrew her terrible form and revealed her beautiful one.
Holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, his entire body is delicate;
his eyes are filled with compassion, and his lotus-face bears a gentle smile.
Having seen that beautiful form, they were then freed from fear;
with peaceful minds, they bowed down, their voices choked with the sound of joyful tears.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Devīgītā—
thus, in the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, the thirty-third chapter of the Devīgītā.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The Seventh Book: Now the Thirty-Fourth Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
Where indeed are you, so unfortunate, and where is this most wonderful form? Nevertheless, out of affection for my devotees, such a sight has been shown by me.
This form cannot be seen through the study of the Vedas, nor through yogic practices, nor by means of gifts, austerity, or sacrifice; it is possible only through my compassion alone.

Listen to the subject at hand, O Indra among kings: here, the Supreme Self, through association with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), assumes the state of a living being as well as agency and other such qualities.
One performs various actions, which have dharma and adharma as their sole causes;
having thereby entered various wombs, one is joined with pleasure and pain.
Furthermore, due to the power of those formative forces (*saṃskāra*), one is always engaged in various activities;
one attains various bodies and is joined with pleasure and pain.
Indeed, like a water-wheel, there is never a cessation for this [cycle];
ignorance alone is its root, from which arises desire, and from that, actions.
Therefore, a person should strive with constancy for the destruction of ignorance;
for this indeed is the fulfillment of birth: the destruction of ignorance.
The fulfillment of the goals of human existence and even the state of liberation while living are accomplished by knowledge alone;
indeed, it is knowledge that is most powerful in destroying ignorance.
O Mountain, because there is no contradiction, ritual action does not obstruct that [meditation] born of that;
on the contrary, once the ignorance of desire is destroyed, there can be no further need for ritual action.
For indeed, harmful actions yearn for one again and again;
from that comes passion, from that comes hatred, and from that great misfortune arises.
Therefore, with every effort, a person should accomplish knowledge;
yet, because it is said, "even while performing actions here," action is also indispensable.
For liberation arises from knowledge alone; therefore, there should be a combination of them.
Karma, being beneficial, may serve as an auxiliary to knowledge.
Thus some say here that [liberation] could not occur because of the contradiction;
for the breaking of the knot of the heart would result from knowledge, yet the arising of karma occurs when the knot of the heart exists.
Simultaneity is not possible for those two because of their contradiction,
just as simultaneity is impossible for darkness and light.
Therefore, O Great-minded One, all Vedic rites should culminate in the purification of the mind; one should perform them with diligent effort.
Tranquility, self-control, endurance, and dispassion arise from the quality of goodness (sattva);
ritual actions exist only up to that limit, and not beyond it.

At the conclusion of that [practice], the self-possessed one, having renounced all else, should again take refuge with a guru who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman, with sincere devotion.
One should constantly listen to the Vedānta in this manner, free from sloth;
one should perpetually investigate the meaning of such statements as "That thou art."
But the statement "That thou art" and others reveal the identity of the individual soul and Brahman;
once this identity is known, one becomes fearless and is indeed born in my own form.
First comes the comprehension of word-meanings, and from that, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning;
I have proclaimed this to you as the meaning of the word *pada*.
And the meaning of the word "thou" (tvaṃ-pada) is none other than the living being (jīva); of this there is no doubt.
The identity of these two is declared by the wise through the word "is" (asi). (Dg 4.21 = DbhP 7,34.21)
Because the two expressed meanings are contradictory, their identity cannot possibly be established;
therefore, one must employ figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for those two realities situated within the scripture. (Dg 4.22 = DbhP 7,34.22)
Pure consciousness alone is the objective referent (lakṣya) of those two; thus, the possibility of their identity exists.
Having realized the identity of those two in such a way, one becomes non-dual through non-distinction from oneself.
The recognition that "this is that very Devadatta" is known as *pratyabhijñā* (recognition);
thus, a person, freed from the body and its attributes such as grossness, attains Brahman.
The gross body is produced from the fivefold great elements;
it is the locus of experience, joined with old age and disease, and [the substrate] of all karmas.
This which appears clearly is false because it consists of illusion;
O Lord of Mountains, this is that gross limitation (upādhi) of my self.
The wise know that subtle body to be endowed with the organs of knowledge and action, joined with the five vital breaths, and possessed of mind and intellect.

This subtle body (sūkṣmadeha) of the self, arising from the unquintuplicated elements (apañcīkṛtabhūta), is the second limiting adjunct (upādhi); it is that which brings about the cognition of pleasure and so forth.
O Lord of Mountains, this third [state] is ignorance (*ajñāna*), beginningless and indescribable;
it appears as this body, the causal self (*kāraṇātman*) of the Self.
When the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) has occurred, the absolute Self alone remains;
yet within the three bodies, the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) are always present.
Upon the relinquishing of the five sheaths, the tail of Brahman is indeed attained—
that form of mine which is described by such statements as "not this, not this."
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it has not ceased to exist. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
If one thinks to kill what is already killed, or if one thinks that what is killed has been killed, both of them do not understand; for this [Self] neither kills nor is killed.
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the secret cave of this living being;
through the grace of the Creator, one who is free from desire beholds Him and His majesty, and is thus liberated from sorrow.
Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself;
know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins.
The wise say that the senses are the horses and their objects are the paths;
the self, joined with the senses and the mind, they call the enjoyer.
But he who is ignorant, lacks mental discipline, and is always impure,
does not attain that state and instead enters into the cycle of existence.
But he who possesses discernment, who is possessed of a focused mind and is always pure,
attains that state from which he is not born again.
But that man who has consciousness as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the path— that supreme state which is mine.
Having thus ascertained the self by means of oneself through both scripture and reasoning,
one should meditate upon me, who am identical with the nature of the self, even through profound contemplation.
Prior to the practice of yoga, one should contemplate the three syllables within oneself for the purpose of meditating upon the two things expressed by the mantra known as the Goddess-Pranava.
The syllable *ha* is the gross body; the syllable *ra* is the subtle body;
the syllable *ī* is that causal self; and the syllable *hrīṃ* is the fourth state, the "I" (*aham*).
Having thus understood the three seed-syllables in sequence within the collective body as well,
the wise person should contemplate the unity of the collective and the individual.
But having first meditated thus with devotion prior to the time of formal concentration,
one should then, with eyes closed, contemplate me, the Goddess, the Sovereign of the World.
Having made the out-breath and in-breath equal as they move within the nostrils,
with desire for sense objects ceased, free from defects, and devoid of envy.
Endowed with sincere devotion, in a cave or in a place free from noise,
one should dissolve the universal self, which is the syllable *ha*, into the syllable *ra*.
One should dissolve the fiery deity represented by the syllable *ra* into the syllable *ī*;
one should dissolve the wise self (*prājña-ātman*) represented by the syllable *ī* into the syllable *hrīṃ*.

One should meditate within the crest-lock upon that which is devoid of the relationship between the signified and the signifier, free from dualistic existence, indivisible, and consisting of being, consciousness, and bliss.
Thus, O King, by means of meditation, that best of men, having directly realized me,
becomes my very form, since there is oneness between the two.
Having seen me, the Self who is higher than the highest, by means of this yoga-method,
that very moment shall be the destroyer of ignorance along with its effects.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Devīgītā;
thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The Seventh Book: Now the Thirty-fifth Chapter. Himālaya said:
O Great Goddess, I know the Yoga along with its limbs, which bestows pure consciousness;
by performing it, may I become fit for the vision of reality.
The Goddess said:
"Yoga is not on the back of the sky, nor on the earth, nor in the subterranean realm (rasātala);
those expert in yoga declare that the union of the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman) is yoga."
O sinless one, their six obstacles have been declared to be the creators of hindrances to yoga:
desire and anger, greed and delusion, and those known as pride and envy.
By means of the very limbs of yoga, having broken through those [obstacles], yogins shall attain yoga:
restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and thereafter [withdrawal, concentration, meditation, and absorption].
Withdrawal of the senses, that which is called retention, meditation, together with meditative absorption—
these they call the eight limbs for the practice of yoga by yogins.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion,
uprightness, patience, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity— these are the ten restraints (yamas).
Austerity, contentment, faith, generosity, worship of the deity,
listening to the established doctrine, modesty, intelligence, recitation, and burnt offerings.
O leader of mountains, these ten observances have been proclaimed by me:
the lotus posture (padmāsana), the auspicious posture (svastika), the fortunate posture (bhadra), and likewise the thunderbolt posture (vajrāsana).
This is declared to be the *vīrāsana*; thus, in sequence, the five postures [are described]. Having properly placed the soles of the auspicious feet upon the thighs— Dg_5.9 = DbhP_7,35.9.
Then, one should bind the two thumbs with the hands in reverse order;
this is called the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), which is dear to the hearts of yogins.
Having properly placed the auspicious soles of the feet between the knees and thighs, the yogi should enter with an upright body; that is called the *svastika* posture.
Having firmly placed the pair of ankles on both sides of the seam [of the perineum],
one should bind the heels beneath the scrotum with those two heels.
This is called the *bhadrāsana*, highly honored by yogins:
having placed the feet successively upon the thighs, with the knees facing outward and the fingers turned inward.
One should place the hands as described; this is the unsurpassed vajrāsana.
Having placed one foot below, one should likewise rest the thigh upon the other.
The yogi, with body straight, should enter the *vīrāsana* posture as it is called;
he should draw in the external air through the *iḍā* [nāḍī] for sixteen *mātrās*.
The yogi should retain [the breath] when full for sixty-four measures,
properly within the center of the *suṣumnā*, slowly for thirty-two measures.
The best among those who know yoga should exhale through the piṅgalā channel;
those learned in the yoga scriptures call this prāṇāyāma.
In this manner, one should practice the external [breathing] for him again and again in succession;
the increase in measure should be done gradually, correctly reaching twelve and then sixteen [mātrās].

The wise know that breath control (prāṇāyāma) together with recitation, meditation, and so forth, to be "with essence" (sagarbha); they know that which is devoid of these to be "without essence" (vigarbha).
For a person practicing in succession, the emergence of sweat in the body is considered the lowest [stage];
that accompanied by trembling is the middling; and the abandonment of the ground is regarded as the highest.
The attainment of the highest qualities is held to last as long as one practices restraint over the senses that roam unimpeded among their objects.
The forceful withdrawal from those [objects] is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
[It is practiced] at the thumbs, ankles, knees, thighs, *mūlādhāra*, genitals, and navel.
In the regions of the heart, neck, and throat, then in the uvula, in the nose,
between the eyebrows, on the forehead, at the crown of the head, and at the dvādaśānta, according to the prescribed rule.
The retention of the vital breath is called *dhāraṇā*,
performed with a concentrated mind abiding within consciousness.
Meditation here is said to be the visualization of one's chosen deity within oneself,
and the constant cultivation of the equality between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
The sages have declared that samādhi is characterized by eight limbs;
now I shall explain to you the unsurpassed yoga of mantra.
O Mountain, it is said that the "All" (viśva) is the body, consisting of the five elements;
through the splendors of the moon, sun, and fire, it is the form of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman.
It is held that there are thirty-five million channels in the body;
among them, ten are declared to be primary, and from among those, three are established as the most essential.
Here, within the spinal column (merudaṇḍa), the primary channel has the form of the tips of the moon and sun;
the white channel Iḍā is situated on the left, having the form of the moon.
That channel, however, is in the form of Śakti, the very embodiment of nectar;
that which is on the right, named Piṅgalā, is in the form of Puruṣa, the embodiment of the Sun.
That Suṣumnā, consisting of all splendor, has the form of fire;
in its center, within that which is called Vicitra, reside the essences of will, knowledge, and action.
In the center is the self-arisen liṅga, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
above that is the seed-syllable of Māyā, whose essence is Hara, consisting of the bindu and nāda.
Above that, however, is Kuṇḍalī, shaped like a crest, with a red body;
she is said to be of the nature of the Goddess, O Lord of Mountains, and non-different from me.
Outside of that, one should visualize a lotus with four petals beginning with the letters *va* and ending with *sa*, having the appearance of gold and shining like molten gold.
Above that is the unsurpassed Svādhiṣṭhāna, resembling fire, having six petals with the brilliance of a diamond, and consisting of the six syllables beginning with *ba* and ending with *la*.
The root is the six-cornered base; therefore they know it as the *mūlādhāra*.
By the word "self" (*sva*), they know the supreme *liṅga* as the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
Above that, at the region of the navel, is the Maṇipūra [cakra], which possesses great radiance;
it has the luster of clouds and the brilliance of lightning, and is composed of manifold splendor.
That lotus, being split like a jewel, is likewise called a "jewel-lotus" (maṇipadma);
it is endowed with ten petals and is possessed of the letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha*.
The lotus presided over by Viṣṇu is the cause for the vision of Viṣṇu;
above that is the Unstruck (anāhata) lotus, resembling the rising sun.
One [lotus] is established with petals corresponding to the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*;
in its center is a *bāṇaliṅga*, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
There, the unstruck sound (anāhata), consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), is perceived;
that lotus is celebrated by the sages as being called "unstruck" (anāhata).
That is the abode of bliss, supreme and presided over by the Puruṣa;
above that is the petal known as Viśuddha, a sixteen-petaled lotus.
Endowed with sixteen vowels, smoke-colored and of great radiance,
it is called *viśuddha* because it extends from the perception of the world as a *haṃsa* by the living being.
The pure lotus is said to be called "Space," most wonderful;
above that is the wheel of command (ājñācakra), supreme and presided over by the Self.
The transmission of the command occurs therein; therefore, it is proclaimed as "the Command" (ājñā).
That most beautiful lotus consists of two petals joined with the letters *ha* and *kṣa*.
Above that is the one called Kailāsa, and above that is Rodhinī;
thus, O observer of good vows, have the foundational wheels (ādhāracakras) been described to you.
The place of the bindu is said to be ten thousand times ten thousand (yuta) above that;
thus has this entire unsurpassed path of yoga been described.
First, one should join the mind to the foundation (ādhāra) by means of the yoga of inhalation (pūraka).
Between the anus and the genitals lies the power (śakti); by contracting it, one should awaken it.
One should lead [the breath] to the *bindu*-cakra by means of the very sequence of the division of the *liṅgas*;
one should contemplate that supreme power (*parā śakti*) as having become one with Śambhu.
There, having caused that power called Māyā— which is like molten lac and yields the accomplishment of yoga— to drink the nectar arisen therein, [one should proceed].
Having satiated the deities of the six wheels there with a stream of nectar,
the wise one should then bring [it] back to the *mūlādhāra* by that same path.
Even for one practicing in this manner day after day, all the previously mentioned corrupted mantras will certainly be accomplished; it cannot be otherwise.
Just as those qualities which belong to me, the Mother of the World, so too is she liberated from the bonds of existence through old age, death, suffering, and the like. (Dg 5.53 = DbhP 7,35.53)
These qualities certainly arise in the best of practitioners and not otherwise;
thus, my dear, has this supreme wind-concentration been described.
Now listen attentively to me concerning that which is called *dhāraṇā*: having fixed the mind upon the Goddess who is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth.
One quickly becomes absorbed in that through the union of the individual soul and Brahman;
or, if the mind is still defiled, it will not achieve success quickly.
Then, O Mountain, through the application of its constituent parts, the yogi should practice the yogas upon my own limbs,
such as my hands and feet, which are sweet [to behold].
The mantra practitioner should stabilize the mind through mastery over the various stages;
with a purified mind, he should fix the mind upon every form.
O Mountain, as long as the mind remains dissolved in the Goddess, who is pure consciousness,
for that long the practitioner of mantra should practice the recitation of the desired mantra along with fire offerings.
Through the practice of mantra and yoga, one becomes capable of knowing that which is to be known;
for there is no mantra without yoga, nor indeed is there yoga without mantra.
For the yoga of practicing these two is the cause for the perfect realization of Brahman;
just as a jar hidden in a house enveloped by darkness is seen by means of a lamp.
"Thus the self, veiled by illusion, has been made an object of perception by Manu;
in this way, the entire method of yoga, together with its auxiliary limbs, has now been declared by me. (Dg_5.62 = DbhP_7,35.62)
It is to be known through the instruction of the guru, and not otherwise, even by means of millions of treatises.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Devīgītā—
thus in the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the thirty-fifth chapter of the Devīgītā.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The Seventh Book: Now the Thirty-Sixth Chapter. The Goddess said:
O King, with a self thus endowed with such yoga, seated upon his seat, he should meditate upon me in the form of Brahman with sincere devotion.
Manifest, yet dwelling in the secret cave, is the great state;
herein all this is deposited—whatever moves, breathes, and blinks.
Know this as the existent and the non-existent, the most excellent, the supreme beyond discernment, the highest among living beings;
that which is radiant, subtler than the subtle, in which the worlds and the inhabitants of the worlds are established.
This is that syllable, Brahman; it is the vital breath, and it is speech and mind.
This is truth, it is the immortal; O gentle one, know that this is what is to be pierced through.
Taking up the great weapon of the Upaniṣadic bow, one should fix the sharp arrow of contemplation;
drawing it back with a mind absorbed in that state, O gentle one, know that very Imperishable as the target.
The syllable *praṇava* is the bow, the self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be the target.
One must pierce it with undistracted mind; like the arrow, one shall become absorbed in that.
In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, along with the mind and all the vital breaths—know him alone as the one Self; abandon other words. He is the bridge to immortality.
Wherein the channels converge like the spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel,
that very one moves within, being born in manifold ways.
"Om"—thus meditate upon the Self. May there be well-being for you as you cross over to the further shore beyond darkness.
The Self is firmly established in the divine city of Brahman, in the ether.
Consisting of mind, leading the body of vital breaths, it is established in food, having fixed its seat in the heart.
By means of the knowledge of that, the wise behold the immortal form of bliss which shines forth.
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both transcendent and immanent is seen.
In the supreme golden sheath, there shines the radiant, partless Brahman;
that is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self know.
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined.
Brahman alone is this immortal [reality] in the east; Brahman is behind, and Brahman is to the south and to the north.
Spread out below and above, Brahman alone is this entire universe, the most excellent.
He who has such an experience is one who has accomplished his purpose, the best of men;
having become Brahman, with a serene self, he neither grieves nor desires.
O King, fear arises from a second; in the absence of that, one does not fear. There is no separation of that [reality] from me, nor is there any separation of me from it. (Dg 6.16 = DbhP 7,36.16)
"Know for certain, O Parvata, that I am indeed he;
my vision, however, shall be present wherever my wise one resides."
I do not dwell at a sacred ford, nor on Kailāsa, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor anywhere else;
rather, I dwell in the midst of the lotus-heart of those who know me.
A single act of worship by one who possesses my knowledge yields the fruit of ten million acts of my worship;
his lineage becomes pure, and his mother has fulfilled her purpose.
O best of mountains, for one whose mind has its abode in consciousness, the earth is meritorious;
as for that knowledge of Brahman which you have asked about, O most excellent Parvata.
I have explained all of that; indeed, there is nothing further to be said.
This [teaching] is for an eldest son who is endowed with devotion and possesses virtuous conduct.
It should be taught to a disciple who has been described as such, and never otherwise;
[only] to one who possesses supreme devotion toward the deity, and toward the guru just as toward the deity.
For these truths revealed here shine forth for that great-souled one;
he to whom this knowledge has been taught is indeed the Supreme Lord.
He from whom one is unable to perform meritorious deeds, yet who bestows the birth of a Brahmin, is declared to be even more than a father or a mother; therefore, one is his debtor.
"O Mountain, the birth derived from one's father is lost; such a birth as this has never occurred before.
One should not bear malice toward him," so said the Veda as well. (Dg 6.25 = DbhP 7,36.25)
Therefore, according to the established doctrine of the scripture, the Guru who bestows Brahman is supreme;
when Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector, but when the Guru is angry, not even Śaṅkara can save one.
Therefore, O Mountain-Dweller, one should please the glorious Guru with every effort;
through body, mind, and speech, one should always be devoted to him.
Otherwise, however, one would be ungrateful; for there is no atonement for the ungrateful.
This was told by Indra to Atharvan under the threat of decapitation.
When he spoke to the two Aśvins, his head was severed by the wielder of the thunderbolt;
seeing that horse-head lost, the two physicians, the best of gods, [acted].
Then, O Lord of Mountains, those two reattached their own heads to the Sage;
thus, the knowledge of Brahman is to be accomplished through great peril.
"He who has obtained [this] would be blessed and one who has fulfilled his purpose, O Mountain.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa; thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter of the Devīgītā.
Now begins the seventh chapter—
the seventh section—
and now the thirty-seventh chapter.
Himālaya said:
"O Mother, tell me of your own devotion, by which knowledge may indeed arise with ease for this person who is neither of middling capacity nor free from passion."
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Mountains, O Best of Beings, three paths for the attainment of liberation are renowned to me:
the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, and the yoga of devotion."
This is suitable for all three [vehicles] and can be accomplished in every way,
because it is easily accessible, because it is mental in nature, and because it does not afflict the body, mind, and so forth.
That devotion is considered to be of three kinds according to the differences in the qualities of men:
[the first] is that which is directed toward inflicting harm upon others, preceded by hypocrisy.

The devotion of one who is possessed by stinginess and anger is *tāmasī*; whereas that which is free from harming others and the like, and is for the sake of one's own welfare alone, is [of another kind].
Constantly possessed of desire, seeking fame, and greedy for enjoyments,
he worships me with extreme devotion in order to obtain each respective fruit.
But the vulgar person, through the cognition of difference, perceives me as other than himself;
his devotion, O Lord of Mountains, is declared to be of the nature of passion (rājasī).
Action dedicated to the Supreme Lord serves to wash away sins;
because it is prescribed by the Vedas, I must certainly perform it constantly.
One whose intellect is thus resolved, yet who relies upon the notion of duality, performs action for the sake of joy; that devotion, O Naga, is of the nature of goodness (*sāttvika*).
This devotion to the supreme is what leads to attainment, because it relies upon the cognition of non-duality;
for the two types of devotion previously mentioned are not considered to lead to the supreme.
Now, learn from me as I describe supreme devotion:
the constant hearing of my qualities and the recitation of my names.
And may my mind always abide steadily within me— who am a mine of the jewels of virtuous qualities— continuously like a stream of oil.
In that state, no cause whatsoever could ever exist;
nor is there any longing for proximity, equal power, union, or co-residence.
He never knows anything whatsoever that is superior to service to me;
because of the absence of the relationship between server and served, he does not desire liberation therein.
He who, through supreme devotion, reflects upon me alone with vigilance,
knows me constantly as non-different from himself, and not as something separate.
But he who contemplates all living beings as having my own nature develops a love for others just as he does for his own self. (Dg 7.16 = DbhP 7,37.16)
But he who, because of the equality of consciousness, does not make a distinction among those that exist everywhere, in all forms, and at all times; Dg_7.17 = DbhP_7,37.17 //
O Lord, he bows and offers sacrifice even unto the lowest outcaste;
because he has abandoned all sense of duality, he harbors no thought of malice toward anyone whatsoever.
O Lord, may there be faith in beholding my abodes, likewise in beholding my devotees,
faith in hearing my scriptures, and in the mantras, tantras, and so forth.
His mind is always agitated by the madness of love, his body is covered in horripilation,
his eyes are filled with the water of tears of love, and the sound of his voice is choked as it reaches his throat.
He who worships me, the Sovereign, the source of the world, the cause of all causes, with a mind that is truly undivided, O Lord of Mountains— Dg_7.21 = DbhP_7,37.21.
My divine vows, both daily and occasional,
he who performs them constantly with devotion, free from stinginess regarding his wealth, [attains this].
O Mountain, the desire to witness my festival and the performance of my festival likewise arise in him inevitably by his very nature. (Dg 7.23 = DbhP 7,37.23)
Singing my very names aloud, he indeed dances,
free from egoism and the like, and devoid of the identification with the body.
Whatever is performed by the force of past karma (prārabdha) happens in that very way;
I have no concern even regarding such matters as the preservation of the body.
Thus, that which has been described as devotion is remembered as supreme devotion (parabhakti),
in which nothing whatsoever is conceived apart from the Goddess.
O Upholder of the Earth, when such supreme devotion has truly arisen in one,
at that very moment their dissolution occurs within my nature as pure consciousness alone.
That which is the supreme limit of devotion is proclaimed as knowledge itself;
it is also the boundary of detachment, since both of these reside within knowledge.
O Mountain, even for one who has performed devotion, if my knowledge does not arise due to the power of *prārabdha* karma, he goes to Maṇidvīpa.
Having gone there, O Mountain, even though he does not desire them, he experiences all enjoyments;
at the end of that, the knowledge of my nature as consciousness shall arise perfectly for him.
By that [knowledge], one should always be liberated; liberation comes from knowledge and not otherwise.
For one who possesses knowledge right here of the inner self residing within the heart.
The vital breaths of that person who is dependent on my consciousness do not depart;
he attains Brahman itself, for he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself.
It is like gold on the neck, obscured by ignorance;
indeed, through knowledge and the destruction of ignorance, that which was already attained is truly obtained.
O Best of Mountains, my body is other than both the known and the unknown;
it is as it is in a mirror, so it is in the self, as it is in water, so it is in the world of the ancestors.
Just as shade and sunlight are clear and distinct from one another,
even so may my knowledge in this world be free from the state of duality.
But he who, possessing detachment yet lacking wisdom, should die,
would dwell eternally in the Brahma-world for the duration of a kalpa, and thereafter [attain liberation].
Furthermore, his birth shall be in the home of those who are pure and prosperous;
thereafter, he performs the practice, and from that, knowledge indeed arises.
O King, knowledge is attained through many lifetimes, not by means of a single lifetime;
therefore, with every effort, one should apply oneself to the pursuit of knowledge.
Otherwise, there would be a great destruction, and this birth is difficult to obtain again;
even then, for one in the first caste, the attainment of the Vedas is difficult to find.
The perfection of the six qualities beginning with tranquility, as well as the accomplishment of yoga,
and likewise the attainment of a supreme guru— all of this is indeed difficult to find here.
Likewise, through the sharpness of the faculties and the refinement of the body,
the desire for liberation arises from the merits accumulated over many lifetimes.
Even when the means of accomplishment have thus become fruitful,
the life of that man who does not strive for the sake of knowledge is utterly meaningless.
Therefore, O King, one should apply effort according to one's ability for the sake of knowledge;
one certainly obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step.
Like ghee hidden within milk, consciousness dwells within every single being;
it must be constantly churned by the mind acting as the churning stick.
"Having attained knowledge, one becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose"—this is the drumbeat of the Vedānta.
Everything has been stated in brief; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Devīgītā;
thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa;
[now begins] the eighth chapter.
The Seventh Book: Now the Thirty-Eighth Chapter.
Himālaya said:
O Goddess of the Gods, how many places on the surface of the earth are to be visited—
those which are principal, pure, and most beloved by the Goddess?
Likewise, whatever vows grant satisfaction and whatever festivals there may be—
all that, O Goddess, O Mother, is for the sake of the man who has accomplished his purpose.
The Śrī Devī said:
"Everything visible is my abode; all times consist of vows.
Since I am the one who possesses all forms, there are festivals at all times."
Nevertheless, out of affection for my devotees, I shall say something, little by little;
O King of Mountains, listen attentively to my words.
Kolāpura is a great place where Lakṣmī is ever-present;
it is the mother’s second city, supreme and presided over by Reṇukā.
Tulajāpura shall be the third, and likewise Saptashringa;
as well as the great site of Hiṅgulā and that of Jvālāmukhī.
The supreme abode of Śakambharī, the most excellent abode of Bhrāmarī,
the abode of Śrī Raktadantikā, and likewise the abode of Durgā.
The supreme among all supreme places is the abode of her who dwells on the Vindhya mountains;
the great site of Annapūrṇā, the unsurpassed city of Kāñcī.
The supreme abode of Bhīmādevī, as well as the Vimalā abode,
the great abode of Śrī Candralā, and the Kauśikī abode.
The supreme abode of Nīlāmbā is on the peak of the Blue Mountain;
likewise, there is the abode of Jāmbūnadeśvarī and the auspicious Śrīnagara.
The great abode of Guhyakālī is established in Nepal;
and that which is called the supreme abode of Mīnākṣī is in Cidambaram.
Vedāraṇya is a great place presided over by Sundarī;
Ekāmbara is a great place established by Paraśakti.
Likewise, there is the supreme site of Mahālasā and that of Yogeśvarī;
similarly, the site of Nīlasarasvatī is renowned among the Cīnas.
At Vaidyanātha, however, the site of Bagalā is considered the most excellent;
Maṇidvīpa is remembered by me as belonging to the illustrious Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī.
The yoni-maṇḍala of Kāmākhyā belonging to the illustrious Tripurabhairavī is a jewel among sacred fields upon the earth’s surface, consecrated by Mahāmāyā.
There is no place on the surface of the earth superior to this,
where the Goddess herself becomes manifest in her menstrual state month after month.
All the deities residing there have attained the nature of mountains;
even the great deities dwell within the mountains themselves.
The entire earth there is considered by the wise to be the form of the Goddess;
there is no place higher than this, the maṇḍala of the womb called Kāmākhya.
The supreme abode of the Gāyatrī is said to be the illustrious Puṣkara;
Caṇḍikā resides at Amareśa, and Puṣkarekṣiṇī at Prabhāsa.
In the great place of Naimiṣa, that goddess is Liṅgadhāriṇī;
she is Puruhūtā in Puṣkarākṣa, and likewise Rati in Aṣāḍha.
In the great place of Caṇḍamuṇḍī, she is the supreme goddess Daṇḍinī;
in Bhārabhūti she is Bhūti, and in Nakula she is Nakuleśvarī.
Candrikā is remembered as Śāṅkarī in Hariścandra on Mount Śrī;
she is Triśūlā at Japyeśvara, and Sūkṣmā at Āmrātakeśvara.
Śāṅkarī is at Mahākāla; Śarvāṇī is in the one called Madhyama;
and in the great field known as Kedāra, that goddess is the Bestower of the Path.
She is known as Bhairavī in the place called Bhairava; she is remembered as Maṅgalā in Gayā;
she is Sthāṇupriyā in Kurukṣetra; and she is also [present] in Svāyambhuva and Nākula.
Ugrā is at Kanakhala, Viśveśā at Vimaleśvara;
Mahānandā is at Aṭṭahāsa, and Mahāntakā is at Mahendra.
In Bhīma she is called Bhīmeśvarī; furthermore, in the place of Vastrāpatha she is called Bhavānī Śāṅkarī; and in Ardhakoṭika she is called Rudrāṇī.
The large-eyed one is in Avimukta; the highly fortunate one is in Mahālaya;
Bhadrakarṇī is in Gokarṇa; and Bhadrā is in Bhadrakarṇaka.
Utpalākṣī is in Suvarṇākṣa; Sthāṇvīśā is in the place known as Sthāṇu;
Kamalā is in Kamalālaya; and Pracaṇḍā is in Chagalaṇḍaka.
In Kuraṇḍala there is Trisandhyā; in Mākoṭa, Mukuṭeśvarī;
in Maṇḍaleśa, Śāṇḍakī; and furthermore, Kālī is in Kālañjara.
Sound is said to reside in Śaṅkukarṇa; it becomes gross in Sthūlakeśvara.
In the heart-lotus of the wise, the Supreme Goddess is Hṛllekhā.
These places have been declared to be most beloved by the Goddess;
having first heard of the majesty of each respective sacred field, O best of mountains.
Thereafter, one should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite;
or else, O best of mountains, all sacred fields exist within Kāśī.
There he should dwell constantly, ever devoted to the worship of the Goddess,
beholding those sacred sites and reciting the mantra to the Goddess without interruption.
Meditating upon those lotus feet, one is liberated from bondage;
whoever recites these names of the goddesses after rising in the morning [shall attain this].
O Mountain, sins are reduced to ashes at that very instant;
one should quickly recite these pure verses before the foremost of the twice-born during the time of a śrāddha ceremony.
All those ancestors of yours, being liberated, proceed to the supreme goal.
Now, O you of excellent vows, I shall describe the observances to you.
Both women and men should diligently perform the vow known as Anantatṛtīyā, the Rasakalyāṇinī vow.
The vow known as Ārdrānandakara on the third lunar day,
the Friday vow, and likewise the Kṛṣṇacaturdaśī.
Therein lies the vow of the day of Mars (Bhaumavāra) as well as the vow of Pradoṣa,
where the Great God (Mahādeva), having seated the Goddess upon a throne, [performs the rite].
At the onset of night, she dances before [the deity] together with the gods;
having fasted there, one should worship Śivā at the beginning of the night, during Pradoṣa.
O Mountain, the Somavāra-vrata is especially an antidote and brings great pleasure to that Goddess; it is exceedingly dear to me.
There too, having fully worshipped the Goddess, one should take a meal at night;
this vow, observed for two nine-night periods, is pleasing [to her].
O Lord, likewise, he who is free from envy performs other constant and occasional vows for the sake of pleasing me.
He attains union with me; he is my devotee, he is dear to me.
O Lord, he should also perform festivals, including the joy of the swing festival.
Just as you would perform the festival of the couch, so too should you perform for me the festival of the vigil,
the chariot festival, and indeed the festival of *damana*.
My devotee should always perform the Pavitraka festival in the month of Śrāvaṇa, which brings great joy, as well as other great festivals in this manner.

One should feed my devotees with affection, as well as married women, virgins, and young celibates (baṭukas), regarding them with the thought that they are myself, with one's inner being fully absorbed in that.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, one should worship these [deities] with fine incense and other offerings;
whoever performs this with devotion every year, unwearied, [attains the result].
He is blessed, he has accomplished his task, and he is truly a worthy recipient of my affection;
everything that brings me joy has been told to him in brief.
It must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has not been instructed.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Devīgītā—
thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
[Now begins] the ninth chapter.
The Seventh Book: Now the Thirty-ninth Chapter.
Himālaya said:
O Goddess of gods, O Great Sovereign, O Mother who is an ocean of compassion,
please now correctly explain the procedure for your own worship exactly as it is.
The Goddess said:
"O King, O bull among mountains, listen with extreme faith as I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Ambikā in a manner that is pleasing to her."
My worship shall be of two kinds: external and internal as well.
The external is also said to be twofold: Vedic and likewise Tantric.
And the Vaidikī [form] is also of two kinds according to the distinction of its forms, O Supporter of the Earth;
the Vaidikī is to be performed by those who are Vaidikas and endowed with Vedic initiation.
But for those who possess the initiations taught in the Tantras, the Tantric [form] should be resorted to;
otherwise, without knowing the secret of worship in this way, one will act erroneously.
Whatever foolish person performs [this], he falls in every way.
Regarding that, I shall first explain the Vedic method which has been taught.
O Supporter of the Earth, that supreme form which you have seen directly before me is great,
with infinite heads and eyes, and infinite feet.
One should constantly worship, bow down to, meditate upon, and remember that very [reality] which is endowed with all powers, the impeller, and higher than the highest.
Thus, O Mountain, the nature of this first image has been described;
one who is peaceful, with a concentrated mind, and free from hypocrisy and egoism [should perform it].
Be devoted to that, perform sacrifice for that, and go to that alone as your refuge;
behold that alone with your mind, and at all times recite and meditate upon it.
Resorting to my state of being with undivided devotion joined with love,
satisfy me alone through sacrifices, austerities, and gifts.
In this way, through my grace, you shall be liberated from the bonds of existence;
those who are devoted to me, whose minds are attached to me, are considered the best of devotees.
I promise that I shall deliver you from this state of existence before long,
either through meditation joined with action, or again through devotion and knowledge.
O King, I am attained in every way, but not by mere actions alone;
devotion arises from dharma, and through devotion, the Supreme is attained.
That which is proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti is celebrated as Dharma;
that which is taught by other scriptures is called a semblance of Dharma (dharmābhāsa).
The Veda has arisen from me, who am omniscient and omnipotent;
because ignorance is absent in me, the Śruti is not invalid.
And the Smṛtis have emerged only after grasping the meaning of the Śruti;
therefore, the authority of both Manu and others, as well as of the Śrutis, is accepted.

Sometimes and in certain places, they speak of a dharma proclaimed by others through a glance toward the meaning of the Tantras; however, that partial [teaching] must not be accepted by those who follow the Vedas.
Because other authors of treatises arise from ignorance and their teachings are corrupted by the fault of ignorance, their words lack authoritative validity.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should in every way rely upon the Veda for the sake of dharma;
and just as a royal decree in the world is never transgressed, so too [should the Veda be followed].
That command of mine, which is the supreme authority of all, is the sacred revelation; how could it be rejected by men?
Indeed, the castes of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas exist for the sake of preserving my command.
Therefore, it should be known that this secret word of my Śruti was created by me:
"For whenever there is a decline of Dharma, O Supporter of the Earth..."
When there was the rise of unrighteousness, I then assumed various guises;
it was for this very reason, O King, that the distinction between gods and daityas came into being.
For those who do not practice that Dharma for the sake of its training,
I have constantly prepared hells, so that terror may arise from merely hearing of them.
If anyone should abandon the dharma of the Vedas and take refuge in another dharma,
the king should banish these unrighteous people from his own realm.
They are not to be conversed with by brahmins, nor are they to be admitted into the ritual row by the twice-born;
as for whatever other various scriptures exist in this world, [the same applies].
Those which contradict the Śruti and Smṛti are entirely of the nature of darkness (tāmasa),
such as the Vāma, Kāpālaka, Kaulaka, and the Bhairava Āgamas.
It was brought forth by Śiva for the purpose of deluding [them], and not for any other reason;
[it occurred] due to the curse of Dakṣa, the curse of Bhṛgu, and the curse of Dadhīca.
For the sake of uplifting those excellent brahmins who have been scorched and cast outside the path of the Vedas, [he acts] always by means of a gradual sequence of steps.
The Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Sauras, Śāktas,
as well as the Gāṇapatyas and the Āgamas, were indeed composed by Śaṅkara.
In that regard, even those portions not in conflict with the Vedas have indeed been stated here and there; for those who accept them, no fault whatsoever ever arises.
In no way may a twice-born man be entitled to a meaning that contradicts the Vedas;
however, one who is devoid of entitlement to the Vedas may have entitlement therein.
Therefore, with every effort, one who follows the Veda should take refuge in the Veda;
for knowledge conjoined with dharma reveals the supreme Brahman.
Having abandoned all cravings, they have come to me alone for refuge;
they are compassionate toward all beings and free from pride and egoism.
With their minds fixed on me, their lives surrendered to me, and delighting in discourse concerning my state—
whether they be renunciants, forest-dwellers, householders, or celibate students.
They always worship with devotion the yoga known as the Sovereign;
for them, who are never separated from it, I [dispel] the darkness born of ignorance.
"I shall destroy [it] by the light of the sun of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O Lord of Mountains, is the first of the Vedic worship."
The essential nature has been briefly explained; now I shall speak of the second [practice], whether upon an image, on a sacrificial mound, or likewise within the disks of the sun and moon.

Having meditated upon the Goddess, who is higher than the highest, either in water, or on a *bāṇaliṅga*, or on a yantra, or on a great cloth, or likewise in the lotus of the heart of Śrī; Dg_9.39 = DbhP_7,39.39.
She possessed all auspicious marks, was full of compassion, youthful, and as red as the rising sun;
she was the ultimate limit of the essence of beauty, beautiful in every limb.
I bow to the Mother, who is filled with the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), who is ever distressed by the suffering of her devotees,
whose face is gracious, and who wears a crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
One should worship her, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, whose nature is bliss, with ritual offerings according to one's means.
As long as one does not possess the qualification for internal worship, one should rely upon this external worship; but once that [qualification] has arisen, one should abandon it.
But that which is internal worship is known as the dissolution into consciousness;
consciousness alone is my supreme form, free from all limiting adjuncts.
Therefore, one should fix the mind without support upon consciousness, which is my own nature;
for the world, which is beyond the form of consciousness, is false and composed of illusion.
